resources.string: How the ribs and sternum move with breathing
A qualitative view of normal quiet breathing. Motion is enlarged for clarity; angles, dimensions, and timing are not measurements.

The ribs attach to the thoracic spine at the back. At the front, the top seven pairs reach the sternum through their own costal cartilages. The next three join the costal margin; the last two pairs have no front attachment.
The sternum lifts and moves forward
As you breathe in, the front ends of the upper ribs rise and carry the sternum up and forward. This pump-handle component increases the depth of the chest from front to back.
The sides of the ribs swing outward

During the same breath, the curved sides of the ribs lift and swing outward, widening the chest from left to right. This bucket-handle component is easy to see along the lower ribs. Each rib can combine both kinds of motion around an oblique axis near the spine.
The chest gains room in three directions
The rib cage deepens and widens while the contracting diaphragm descends and flattens, adding height to the chest cavity. Together these changes increase chest volume, and the lungs expand with it.
The chest returns during quiet exhalation

Quiet exhalation is mostly passive. The diaphragm relaxes and rises into a dome. The chest returns toward its resting size through elastic recoil, and air flows out. The lungs do not empty completely.
